Subject: SLO / monitoring questionnaire for procurement

Hi Sofia and Rishi,

Thanks for taking the time to work with Nebula's procurement/SRE team. As part of our procurement review we need detailed answers on how Redwood measures and exposes SLOs (uptime/latency), your monitoring/alerting practices, and the process for approving exceptions or temporary SLA relaxations.

Please provide the following items where possible:
- Formal SLO definitions (availability windows, error classes included/excluded) and the measurement window used (rolling 30d, calendar month, etc.)
- Latency SLOs (p50/p95/p99) for the API and any separate SLOs for streaming endpoints
- Instrumentation and telemetry sources used to compute SLOs (synthetic probes, server-side sampling, client-side telemetry)
- How alerts are generated and routed (PagerDuty, email, ticket creation) and typical escalation timelines
- Whether Nebula customers can access raw or aggregated metrics (Prometheus endpoints, read-only dashboards, Grafana links) and any RBAC limits
- Data retention for metrics and logs used for SLO computation
- The formal exception process for bursts, initial warm-up, or planned maintenance (criteria, maximum duration, approval authority)
- Any recent exceptions or rollbacks in the past 12 months (summary OK)

We attached a short PDF with the procurement questionnaire for you to fill; if you prefer, a Drive link or short call works too. Would appreciate a response by EOD Friday 2026-09-03 to keep the contract review on schedule.

Thanks,
Emma Park
Procurement Manager, Nebula AI
procurement@nebulaai.com

Hi Emma — thanks for the clear checklist. I've completed a first-pass response below and attached a CSV with the metric names we use to compute SLOs. Mina (Engineering Manager, Production Reliability) is looped in for the exception process and approvals.

Quick answers (summary):
- Measurement window: rolling 30-day window by default for operational SLOs; we also report calendar-month aggregates on request.
- Availability SLO: 99.95% measured as successful request ratio (2xx responses) excluding planned maintenance windows and certified force majeure incidents.
- Latency SLOs (text generation API, typical model routes): p50 < 120ms, p95 < 420ms, p99 < 900ms for token response latency under standard contract profiles. For streaming endpoints we have separate p50/p95 targets (streaming p95 < 600ms chunk latency).
- Instrumentation: primary source is server-side telemetry collected from the serving runtime (per-request metrics). We augment with synthetic probes (external probes from three regions) to capture network/edge variability. Sampling: all requests are counted for availability; latency SLO uses 1:50 sampled traces for tracing and full histogram collection at the service level.
- Alerts: SLO burn-rate alerting using a rolling window and predefined burn thresholds; critical alerts route to PagerDuty with 15-minute escalation, high/medium alerts open a ticket in Jira automatically and notify the assigned account engineer.
- Customer access: customers get a read-only Grafana dashboard and a Prometheus-compatible read endpoint (API key-scoped, read-only). Dashboards include SLO time series, error taxonomy, and recent incidents. We can provide a drive link to the dashboard export for procurement review.
- Retention: metrics retention is 13 months at full resolution; aggregated summaries are retained for 24 months. Trace samples are kept for 90 days.
- Exception process: exceptions (e.g., burst-induced p99 inflation, onboarding warm-up) are handled via an Exception Request document submitted to Production Reliability. Short-lived operational exceptions (<7 days) can be approved by the Reliability Manager; exceptions >7 days or that affect contractual uptime must be approved by VP Engineering and Legal, and documented to customers with a rollback plan.
- Recent exceptions: in the past 12 months we approved two planned exceptions during major model rollouts (noted in the attached CSV summary).

Attachments: redwood_slo_metrics_descriptions.csv (metric -> definition -> collection method)

I'll follow up with a short screen share to show the read-only Grafana view if helpful. If Emma needs a formal signed addendum for the exception terms, loop in Legal and we can draft it.

Best,
Rishi Malhotra
Senior Account Executive

Folks, quick internal note to align before we send any formal exception wording to Nebula:

- Approval authority: Reliability Manager (me) can approve operational exceptions <=7 days for onboarding/warm-up. Anything longer or any exception that touches the historical uptime calculation (i.e., we would exclude a period from contract uptime) needs sign-off from VP Eng and Legal.
- Scope and limits: exceptions are scoped to specific routes/models/regions. They are not global unless explicitly agreed. For example, a warm-up exception for Nebula's dedicated pool could be scoped to the model: "gptx-4dence-2026" for 14 days with step-down targets.
- Communication: we produce an Exception Request doc with: reason, affected routes, start/end, mitigation steps, expected impact (p50/p95/p99 delta), monitoring plan, and rollback criteria. We publish that to the customer-facing incident link and also add to contract addendum if requested.
- Data used for approval: 30d rolling SLO graphs, a pre-rollout synthetic probe baseline, and initial load test results.

Sofia — can you prepare the short Exception Request template and a one-page customer-facing summary? Rishi — let's propose a temporary warm-up exception of up to 10 days (we can reduce if early telemetry stabilizes), and ask Emma whether they need the exception to be documented in the contract or if a standalone operational notice suffices.

Mina Haddad
Engineering Manager, Production Reliability
Redwood Inference
